sampleAnswers.answer: Queens made a real but largely supporting contribution to the reunification of Egypt. Their influence was greatest in the war against the Hyksos, when a royal woman could hold the family’s claim together, and in the religious and dynastic legitimacy that the Eighteenth Dynasty drew on afterwards. The military victories that expelled the Hyksos and reunited the Two Lands were won by the kings, so the queens’ contribution was substantial but secondary. The clearest case is Ahhotep I, mother of the brothers Kamose and Ahmose. A stela set up in her honour credits her with looking after Egypt in a time of conflict and with caring for its soldiers, and her burial contained gold flies and axes of the kind given to soldiers for valour. These objects suggest that she was seen as a war leader. She is generally thought to have acted as regent at Thebes while her sons campaigned against Avaris, and her role in holding the Theban power base together was essential. Whether she commanded in the field is unknown, but her authority in the war years is well attested. Ahmose-Nefertari contributed differently. As Ahmose’s wife she was linked with the god Amun of Thebes at a time when the cult was rising in importance, and later tradition honoured her as a pious and powerful queen. Her religious role connected the new dynasty with the god whose temple at Karnak the kings enlarged, helping to legitimate a family that had risen from Thebes. Tetisheri, Ahmose’s grandmother, gave the line a royal ancestry that the family could use to claim the throne. These contributions shaped the dynasty’s image without deciding its wars. The limits of the queens’ contribution should be stated. Almost all surviving evidence was commissioned by kings or by male officials, so queens appear mainly as honoured family members in stelae and tomb equipment rather than as decision-makers, and historians must infer their influence from indirect evidence. Reunification was decided on campaigns that the kings led, against the Hyksos at Avaris and in the southern and Nubian territories, and the kings controlled the army and the administration. A queen’s support could strengthen a campaign, but it could not replace the king’s command of the troops. The queens’ roles also changed with the dynasty’s needs. Once the Hyksos were gone and the Eighteenth Dynasty was secure, the emphasis moved from wartime support to the religious and dynastic image of the royal family, which was displayed in temples at Thebes. This suggests that queens were most useful to the dynasty when its legitimacy was in question, and less visible once victory had secured it. The contrast with the Amarna period, when Nefertiti was prominent in royal art, shows how far queenly visibility depended on the circumstances of each reign. On balance, queens contributed significantly, though indirectly. Ahhotep I’s regency and her sons’ dependence on Theban loyalty, Ahmose-Nefertari’s religious prominence and the dynasty’s use of its ancestry all helped make reunification possible. Yet the decisive military and political action was the kings’, and the queens are best understood as supporting that work rather than driving it. The contribution is therefore real but secondary, and its extent depends on how much weight is given to evidence that is limited and shaped by royal propaganda.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it gives a sustained judgement on ‘to what extent’, uses evidence on Ahhotep I, Ahmose-Nefertari and Tetisheri, and argues from the limits of that evidence. To go further, it could test the claim about Ahhotep’s regency against a named source more directly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Queens contributed to the reunification of Egypt in some ways, although the kings were more important. Ahhotep I is the clearest example. She was the mother of Ahmose and probably held authority at Thebes while her sons fought the Hyksos, and a stela set up for her praises her care for Egypt. This shows a queen in a position of authority during the war years, which supported the family’s claim to the throne. Ahmose-Nefertari also helped the dynasty. As Ahmose’s wife she was connected with the cult of Amun, which was important at Thebes, and this religious role gave the new dynasty legitimacy. Tetisheri, Ahmose’s grandmother, was remembered as an ancestor, so the family could present a long line of royal claims. However, the kings did the fighting. Ahmose drove the Hyksos out of Avaris and campaigned in the south and in Nubia, and it was his army that restored the north. Queens could support the war but could not command the army themselves. The evidence for queens is also limited because most inscriptions were made by kings, so it is hard to say how much queens actually decided. Their support was also visible in the religious life of the court. Ahmose-Nefertari’s association with Amun gave the dynasty a religious message that complemented the king’s military success. Because the kings depended on the god for victory, a queen who served the cult could show that the royal family was pious and blessed. This made the queen a useful partner in the dynasty’s claims, even though the decisions remained with the king. Overall, queens helped reunification mainly through religion and family legitimacy, while the kings made the military decisions. Their contribution was important but was not the most important one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 11–15 row: it gives some judgement, refers to evidence from a stela and to the cult of Amun, and writes in a structured way with some terms. To lift it, sustain the judgement through the body paragraphs and assess the stela as evidence rather than describing it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Queens helped the kings of Egypt during the reunification. Ahhotep was an important queen who looked after the country while her sons were fighting, and a stela records her care for Egypt. Ahmose-Nefertari was also an important queen and was linked with the god Amun. The kings were the main leaders, but the queens had some influence on the family and on the reunification. The queens were also remembered by later generations, which shows that their families valued them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ‘warrior pharaoh’ image was important for the New Kingdom monarchy, though its importance lay more in ideology than in the day-to-day conduct of war. The image justified the kings’ right to rule, explained the empire that Egypt held in Nubia and the Levant, and gave rulers a public role that could be displayed in temples. Its significance must be weighed against the fact that the image was carefully constructed, and that other aspects of kingship, especially religious ones, competed with it. The image mattered because royal legitimacy rested on maintaining order, or ma’at, against foreign enemies. The period began with the expulsion of the Hyksos, a narrative that made the king a liberator, and the kings who followed were shown as heirs of that victory. Scenes of the king smiting enemies, which became a standard subject on temple walls, presented the pharaoh as the guarantor of Egypt’s security. Such images were repeated across Karnak and other temples, so their message reached officials, priests and the wider population who could see them. The clearest expression came under Thutmose III, whose annals carved at Karnak describe his campaigns with a strong sense of personal command. His account of the battle of Megiddo, where he is said to have led the attack in person, shaped how later Egyptians remembered him. The image was important because it reinforced an empire that relied on tribute and on loyal vassal rulers in the Levant. Without some display of military success, the kings could not easily claim the tribute, the gold from Nubia or the loyalty of the local princes on which Egyptian power depended. The image was not the only or the dominant form of kingship. Hatshepsut, who ruled in the same period, presented herself as king in traditional forms, but her monuments at Deir el-Bahari emphasised divine birth, building and the expedition to Punt, and a warrior image was less prominent in her programme. Thutmose IV, whose claim to the throne rested on a dream recorded on a stela between the paws of the Great Sphinx at Giza, also emphasised divine favour. These cases show that rulers chose which aspects of kingship to display, and that the war image was one option among several. The image also shaped how officials understood their roles. A king shown leading his troops encouraged the loyalty of an army whose officers were rewarded by royal favour, so the image tied military service to the crown rather than to any single commander. This made the warrior image a practical tool of government as well as a claim about the king’s character. Its effect on the elite was therefore as important as its effect on the wider population. The importance of the image is best assessed by its effects. It helped legitimise rulers whose claims were not always strong, justified the cost of an empire and encouraged officials to see military service as honourable. But it was constructed for particular audiences, and historians must treat royal accounts of victories with caution because they stress royal valour while the army, the chariot corps and local administrators did much of the work. Overall, the warrior image was important for legitimacy and ideology, and its significance was greatest where it reinforced the monarchy’s control of the empire, but it was one element of a broader kingship rather than its defining feature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it assesses the image’s importance rather than narrating campaigns, uses the Karnak annals and the Hatshepsut and Thutmose IV counter-cases, and gives a qualified judgement. To go further, it could compare the strength of the image in the Karnak annals with its treatment in the reliefs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The warrior pharaoh image was important to the New Kingdom kings because it presented them as protectors of Egypt. Ahmose drove out the Hyksos, and scenes of kings defeating enemies on temple walls showed that the pharaoh could defend the country. This gave the monarchy legitimacy at a time when Egypt was building an empire in Nubia and the Levant. Thutmose III is the best example. His campaigns are recorded in annals at Karnak, and the battle of Megiddo is described as a major victory won by the king in person. These records helped the king show that he was a strong ruler, and they allowed officials and the public to see the empire as the result of royal success. The image therefore supported control of an empire that depended on tribute from vassal rulers. However, the image was not always the most important part of kingship. Hatshepsut, who ruled in the same period, did not stress war in her building programme and was more concerned with trade and religion. Thutmose IV used a dream to claim the throne, which shows that religious legitimacy could be just as important as military success. The image also had practical uses. Showing the king as a successful commander reassured officials that the throne could protect them, and it encouraged soldiers to see their service as a route to royal favour. These purposes gave the image a political value that the reality of each campaign could not fully match. The warrior image was important, but it was one part of how the kings presented themselves. It helped with legitimacy and control of the empire, though other features of kingship mattered as well.

sampleAnswers.answer: The warrior pharaoh image was important in New Kingdom Egypt because the kings had to protect Egypt and show they were strong leaders. Ahmose fought the Hyksos and Thutmose III fought many battles in Syria. The kings showed their victories on temple walls, so people could see them. The image was important for the kings, although they also did other things, such as building temples. The image also appeared in temples, where ordinary Egyptians could see it, so it reached more people than the inscriptions of the elite did.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ramesses II’s contribution to Egypt was considerable, though uneven. He ruled for about sixty-six years, from around 1279 to 1213 BCE, and his reign combined a lasting monumental legacy, a long period of foreign stability and a strong administration. His achievements were partly a matter of image, however, and the evidence for them is largely monumental and propagandistic, which makes it difficult to separate reality from display. His building programme was the most visible contribution. The temples at Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum at Thebes and additions at Karnak and Luxor displayed royal power to Egyptians and visitors and gave the monarchy a lasting presence in the landscape. He also founded Pi-Ramesses in the eastern Delta, a new royal residence close to the Levantine frontier, which reflected the growing importance of the north and of the Near East. These projects were expensive, and their value lay in display as much as in function, but they remain the reign’s clearest legacy. In foreign policy Ramesses preserved and reasserted Egypt’s position. His campaigns in Syria, including the battle of Kadesh, kept key cities and vassal rulers under Egyptian influence, even though Kadesh was not a clear victory. The treaty with Hattusili III secured peace for most of his reign. In Nubia, a network of temples and a viceroy kept the gold-producing region under control. These arrangements gave Egypt stability in its empire for decades. Ramesses also maintained the administration. His long reign produced a stable bureaucracy and a generation of officials who served his successors. His large family, however, brought problems: many of his older sons died before him, and the succession passed to an elderly son, Merenptah, which shows how much the system depended on the king’s personal authority. The strains of the reign were visible in the years after his death. His reign also shows the difficulty of measuring a king’s contribution by monuments alone. The reliefs of Kadesh and the great temples were designed to show a victorious and divinely supported king, and historians must read them as statements of ideology. The administrative records of the period give a fuller picture of how the state worked day to day. They suggest a functioning bureaucracy, but they also show the costs of maintaining a large building programme across the country, which is part of why his achievements look different when viewed from the state rather than from the temple. Ramesses II made a major contribution to Egypt through a long period of stability, a monumental legacy and a durable peace with the Hittites. His achievements were partly a matter of image, and the Kadesh accounts exaggerate his personal role. He preserved the empire and the monarchy’s prestige but did not expand it significantly. His contribution is therefore best assessed as considerable: his building and diplomacy outlived him, although the system he left depended heavily on his own long rule.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it assesses the contribution across building, foreign policy, Nubia and administration, and weighs the image against the reality. To go further, it could test whether the building programme’s cost affected the reign’s later stability with a specific piece of evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ramesses II made a significant contribution to Egypt. He reigned for a very long time and built many temples, including Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, which show his power. These buildings were meant to impress Egyptians and visitors. In foreign policy he kept Egypt’s position in Syria and the Levant. He fought the Hittites at Kadesh and later made a treaty with them. This brought peace for much of his reign. He also controlled Nubia, which was important for gold. He also founded a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, in the Delta. This shows that he thought the north was important. His sons helped run the country, although many of them died before him. His reign also had a long-term effect on how later Egyptians remembered the monarchy. The temples and statues he set up remained visible for centuries, and his name became a standard for royal achievement. This memory shaped later Ramesside kings, who tried to match his scale of building and display. Ramesses II was therefore an important king whose building and foreign policy helped Egypt. His reign was long and gave stability, but some of his achievements were about image rather than real change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 11–15 row: it gives some judgement, uses specific monuments and the treaty, and is structured. To lift it, weigh the achievements against each other and say which contributed most to the state rather than to the king’s image.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ramesses II was an important pharaoh who built a lot, including the temple at Abu Simbel. He fought the Hittites at Kadesh and Egypt was peaceful for a long time after that. He was also a long-reigning king with many children. So he made a contribution to Egypt, mainly through his buildings and his reign. His buildings were also visible to visitors and to later generations, which made them an important part of his legacy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Relations with the Hittites were among the most important foreign questions of the period, though not the only one. The Hittite kingdom controlled Anatolia and contested Egypt’s hold on Syria and the Levant, and the relationship moved from rivalry to a formal peace under Ramesses II. Their importance depends on how it is measured. In terms of Egypt’s territory and long-term stability the Hittite relationship was central, while in terms of wealth and domestic authority, Nubia and the monarchy’s religious position mattered at least as much. The competition was older than Ramesses II. In the Amarna period Egyptian control of Syria weakened as local rulers, such as Aziru of Amurru, turned towards the Hittites, and the Amarna letters record the anxieties of Egyptian vassals who feared abandonment. Suppiluliuma I of Hatti took advantage of this, and Egypt’s inability to protect its Levantine allies left the Hittites in a strong position that Seti I and Ramesses II inherited. Their campaigns in Syria were a response to this threat, and the Hittites were the main obstacle to Egypt’s claim to the region. The Battle of Kadesh, around 1274 BCE, was the defining encounter. Ramesses’ inscriptions present it as a personal triumph in which he rescued a surprised army, but the battle was not decisive. Neither side captured Kadesh, and the Hittites could claim a tactical success. The later treaty of about 1259 BCE, copied in Egyptian at Karnak and the Ramesseum and recorded in a Hittite version on a silver tablet, set out a mutual alliance and recognised the existing frontier. The treaty was arguably more significant than the battle because it produced a long peace that lasted to the end of Ramesses’ reign. Other concerns competed for the monarchy’s attention. Egyptian power in Nubia, which supplied gold and was governed through a viceroy, was just as central to the economy. Internal developments, including the Amarna religious revolution and the later restoration of Amun under Tutankhamun and Horemheb, shaped the monarchy’s authority. Ramesses’ building programmes, funded by the state’s resources, were a source of prestige that did not depend on the Hittites. The Hittite relationship therefore mattered most to foreign policy and the Levant, while other concerns shaped the domestic order. The relationship also had a diplomatic dimension beyond war. Marriage alliances and the exchange of letters between the courts show that the two powers dealt with each other as rulers of equal standing, even while they competed in Syria. Such exchanges meant that the relationship was not only a question of military balance but also of prestige and rank, which Egypt had to maintain in its correspondence. The Hittites’ strength made this recognition necessary, and it shaped the terms in which Ramesses could present his achievements. Overall, relations with the Hittites were very important for Egypt’s position in the Levant and for the long peace of the late reign. They explain the campaigns of Seti I and Ramesses II and the diplomacy that followed. However, they were one element in a wider set of concerns that included Nubia, religion and internal authority, and the peace was as much a result of shared interests and mutual exhaustion as of Egyptian strength. The relationship was therefore a central but not a dominant influence on the period.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it sustains a judgement on ‘to what extent’, uses Kadesh and the treaty as evidence, and weighs the Hittite relationship against Nubia and internal concerns. To go further, it could say more precisely how the treaty’s terms limited Egyptian ambitions in the Levant.

sampleAnswers.answer: Relations with the Hittites were important during this period because the Hittites were Egypt’s main rival in Syria and the Levant. The two powers disputed control of cities such as Amurru and Kadesh, and this rivalry shaped the military policy of Seti I and Ramesses II. The most famous episode is the Battle of Kadesh, fought around 1274 BCE. Ramesses II presented it as a great victory, but the Hittites also claimed success and neither side took the city. The battle shows how difficult the Levant was to control, and the treaty that followed brought peace between the two kingdoms for the rest of Ramesses’ reign. The treaty of about 1259 BCE was an important result. Copies of it were inscribed in Egyptian and Hittite, and the marriage of a Hittite princess to Ramesses showed the new relationship. This reduced the danger of war and allowed Egypt to focus on other areas. The diplomatic contacts also gave Egypt an interest in stability. Once the Hittites could be dealt with through treaty, Egypt could turn to problems in Nubia and at home, which shows how the relationship shaped other priorities. However, relations with the Hittites were not the only important matter. Egypt also had to manage Nubia and its internal religious life. So relations with the Hittites were important, but they were one of several issues.

sampleAnswers.answer: Relations with the Hittites were important to Egypt because the Hittites were a powerful kingdom in Anatolia and they fought Egypt for control of Syria. Ramesses II fought them at the Battle of Kadesh and they later made a peace treaty. This shows that relations were important, although Egypt also had other problems to deal with at home and in Nubia. The relationship mattered because it was a rivalry that ran through the period, and the peace that resulted was an important outcome for both sides.

sampleAnswers.answer: The building of the First Temple was important to Solomon’s reign, but it was only one factor in its success. The Temple gave the Davidic monarchy a religious centre, drew wealth and craftsmanship into Jerusalem and expressed the king’s authority. Its importance must be weighed against the trade and diplomacy that sustained the reign and against the resentment that its labour demands produced. The Temple was central to the reign’s prestige, but it was not the sole cause of its success. The Temple’s most significant contribution was ideological. The biblical account dates the start of building to the fourth year of Solomon’s reign and places it in the four hundred and eightieth year after the Exodus, a chronology historians treat with caution. It says construction took seven years. The Temple was presented as the place for the name of YHWH, and it gave the Davidic dynasty a religious justification that a contested succession could not otherwise provide. A central sanctuary in Jerusalem tied the king to divine favour and made the capital the focus of worship. The Temple also reflected Solomon’s wider achievements. Hiram of Tyre supplied cedar and craftsmen, which shows a commercial and diplomatic partnership that brought skills and wealth to Jerusalem. Solomon’s administrative districts provisioned the court and the building works, and the palace complex, which took longer to build than the Temple, displayed the state’s resources. Trade through the port of Ezion-geber and the supply of horses and chariots show that the reign’s prosperity rested on wider commerce as well as on the Temple. The costs, however, were high. The building programme relied on a labour levy, and the northern tribes resented the burden. After Solomon’s death, their demand for relief from these burdens led to the rejection of Rehoboam and the division of the kingdom. The Temple therefore strengthened the reign’s prestige while contributing to tensions that undermined its unity. The Temple’s importance can also be seen in the way the biblical text connects it to the dynasty’s founder. The narrative presents the building as the fulfilment of David’s intention, so it links Solomon’s reign with David’s legacy. This presentation was itself a claim about legitimacy, and modern readers should note that the account was shaped by later religious and political concerns rather than written as a contemporary record. The judgement about success therefore depends on how far the biblical account is trusted as a guide to the reign’s priorities. The evidence outside the Bible is limited and debated. No inscription from the Temple survives, and scholars disagree over the size of tenth-century Jerusalem and over whether monumental gates and buildings at Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer can be attributed to Solomon. Such debates mean that the Temple’s importance can be argued but not measured precisely. Overall, the Temple was important for the reign’s religious legitimacy and its image of prosperity, but its success depended more on the wider network of trade, diplomacy and administration, and its costs helped to bring about the failure of unity after Solomon.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it weighs the Temple against trade, diplomacy and administration, uses the biblical account while flagging its chronology, and links the costs to the division of the kingdom. To go further, it could assess the Temple’s symbolic importance against its economic cost with a more precise judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The First Temple was important to Solomon’s reign because it gave the monarchy a religious centre in Jerusalem. The Bible describes its construction with help from Hiram of Tyre, who supplied cedar and craftsmen. This shows that the Temple linked the king with divine support and with his foreign partners. The Temple also helped the king’s prestige. Solomon’s reign is remembered for its wealth, and the building of the Temple and the palace showed the resources of the state. The wealth from trade and the chariots also made the kingdom look strong. However, the Temple was not the only reason for the reign’s success. Solomon also made alliances, including a marriage with an Egyptian princess, and he organised the kingdom into districts to feed the court. These policies were probably as important as the building. The Temple also had religious significance that helped the king’s authority. Worship at a single sanctuary in Jerusalem made the capital the centre of the state’s religion, and this gave the monarchy a symbolic focus that other kingdoms did not have in the same form. Such a focus could strengthen the king’s position, but only if the costs of the building programme did not alienate the population. The Temple also had costs. The forced labour that built it caused resentment among the northern tribes, and this contributed to the division of the kingdom after Solomon died. So the Temple was important, but it had a negative side as well.

Solomon was a wealthy king and the Temple shows that he was powerful. However, the Temple caused some problems for the people, so the reign was not completely successful. The Temple was also a visible sign of the king’s wealth, and people who saw it would have connected it with his power.

sampleAnswers.answer: Relations between Israel and Judah were only partly successful in the eighth century BCE. For much of the century the two kingdoms were rivals and occasionally enemies, and their relations were shaped by the pressure of Assyrian expansion. There were periods of relative calm that allowed both to grow, but the fall of Israel and the survival of Judah show that success depended on circumstances the kingdoms could not control. The record is therefore uneven and, for Israel, largely negative. The century opened with open conflict. Around 798 BCE, Amaziah of Judah challenged Jehoash of Israel, and the Judean army was defeated at Beth-Shemesh, where Amaziah was captured and a section of Jerusalem’s wall was broken down (2 Kings 14:8–14). This shows that the power balance favoured Israel. Israel then enjoyed a long period of prosperity under Jeroboam II, roughly 788–747 BCE, and Judah recovered under Uzziah, so both kingdoms could develop, though Judah remained the weaker of the two. The most damaging episode was the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734–732 BCE. Israel and Aram attempted to force Judah under Ahaz into an anti-Assyrian coalition. Ahaz refused and appealed to Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria, who attacked Damascus and the northern kingdom. This relationship allowed Judah to survive by accepting Assyrian overlordship, but it showed that cooperation with a great power could be a success for one kingdom and a disaster for the other. The Assyrian conquest of Samaria in 722 BCE ended the northern kingdom after its rebellion, which was encouraged by Egypt. Judah’s survival after 722 suggests a qualified success. Hezekiah carried out religious reform and strengthened Jerusalem’s defences, and when Sennacherib invaded in 701 BCE the city survived while much of the kingdom was devastated. Some scholars argue that the fall of Samaria drove refugees south and boosted Jerusalem’s growth, although the evidence is debated. The ability of Judah’s kings to adapt to Assyrian pressure allowed the kingdom to survive for more than a century after 701 BCE, though at the cost of vassal status. The relationship also had a moral and religious side. Prophets active in the eighth century, including Amos and Hosea in Israel and Isaiah in Judah, criticised the kingdoms’ social and religious practices and Judah’s dealings with Assyria. These voices show that contemporaries judged the relationship in moral and religious terms as well as political ones, and they often read the disasters of the century as a consequence of the kingdoms’ failings. Whether or not these judgements are accurate, they show that success was measured by more than survival. Overall, relations were successful for Judah in the sense of survival and continued existence under Davidic rule, but largely unsuccessful for Israel, which was destroyed in 722 BCE after its rebellion. The century’s most decisive relationship was less the one between the two kingdoms than the one each had with Assyria. Judah’s success was real but was bought by subordination, and the extent of success is therefore limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it judges success separately for each kingdom, uses specific episodes from the eighth century, and sustains a qualified judgement about Assyria’s role. sampleAnswers.answer: Relations between Israel and Judah were partly successful in the eighth century BCE. The two kingdoms were often rivals, and there was conflict early in the century when Amaziah of Judah was defeated by Jehoash of Israel. This shows that the relationship was not always peaceful. Later in the century the Assyrian threat changed the relationship. In the Syro-Ephraimite war Israel and Aram tried to force Judah to join them against Assyria. King Ahaz refused and asked Assyria for help. This helped Judah survive but meant that Judah accepted Assyrian control. Israel did not survive. Samaria was captured by Assyria in 722 BCE and the northern kingdom came to an end. Israel had rebelled against Assyria, and this was a disaster for the kingdom. The contrast between the two kingdoms is also visible in their fates. Israel’s prosperity under Jeroboam II did not protect it from Assyria, while Judah survived by accepting a subordinate position. This suggests that success in the century depended more on how a kingdom managed Assyria than on its relations with its neighbour. Judah survived the century, and Jerusalem was not captured when Sennacherib attacked in 701 BCE. Hezekiah strengthened the city. So relations were partly successful for Judah.

Judah survived for longer. The Assyrians were a powerful empire and their attacks affected both kingdoms, so the relations between them were not very successful. The prophets of the period also criticised the kingdoms’ conduct, which suggests that contemporaries did not see their relations as a success.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cyrus II’s contribution to the Persian Empire was foundational. He united the Persians, overthrew the Median kingdom and conquered Lydia and Babylon, and he set the pattern of rule that his successors developed. His achievements were decisive, though many of the institutions associated with the empire were developed later, and his reputation was shaped by his own propaganda and by Greek writers. His contribution was essential, but it was the foundation of the empire rather than its completed structure. Cyrus’s military achievements built the empire. He overthrew Astyages of Media around 550 BCE, and the Median kingdom was absorbed into a Persian state that gave the Persians experience of ruling a large, settled population. Croesus of Lydia was defeated around 546 BCE, and Babylon fell in 539 BCE, which brought the Mesopotamian heartland under Persian control. These victories combined conquest with the continued use of existing administrative and religious structures, which made the new empire workable. Cyrus’s policy towards conquered peoples is central to his reputation. The Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian text composed in his name after the conquest of Babylon, presents him as a legitimate king who restored cult images to their sanctuaries and allowed displaced peoples to return home. The biblical book of Ezra gives a similar account of a decree permitting the Judeans to rebuild their temple. Such a policy eased the government of diverse populations and encouraged loyalty. The cylinder also calls him ‘king of the world’, a title that reflects the image he wished to project, so it should be read as propaganda rather than neutral testimony. The founding of the Achaemenid dynasty gave the empire a royal line that claimed descent from Achaemenes and set expectations of continuity. Yet many features most associated with the empire, including the satrapy system and the standardised administration, developed under Darius I. Cyrus’s own administration was probably less systematic, and his death in 530 BCE on campaign against the Massagetae meant that the empire was tested by a succession before its structures were fully in place. Cambyses continued the expansion by conquering Egypt in 525 BCE, which shows that Cyrus’s work could be extended. Cyrus’s reputation also depended on how later peoples remembered him. Greek writers such as Herodotus presented him as a founder whose end was linked to the ambitions of his conquests, and the biblical account gave him a role as the king who enabled the return from exile. These images reflected the interests of the communities that recorded them, and they should be weighed against the Babylonian and Persian evidence when assessing what Cyrus actually achieved. Cyrus’s contribution was fundamental. He created the conquests that gave Persia an empire, established the dynasty that ruled it for over two centuries, and set a model of tolerant rule that later kings used. His achievements were, however, the foundation of an empire whose structure was refined by his successors, and the image of a benevolent conqueror owes much to propaganda that makes his rule appear more humane than the evidence can confirm. On balance, Cyrus’s contribution to the establishment of the empire was essential and was the most important of any single ruler before Darius.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it evaluates Cyrus’s foundational role, reads the Cylinder as propaganda, and separates his achievements from Darius’s later administration. To go further, it could evaluate the Ezra account against the Cylinder more directly as a second source.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cyrus II was very important in establishing the Persian Empire. He defeated the Medes, the Lydians and the Babylonians, and these victories created a large empire. Without him, the Persians would not have had such a big state. Cyrus was also a good ruler to the people he conquered. The Cyrus Cylinder says he returned the gods of Babylon and allowed people to go home. This policy meant that the conquered peoples were not so resistant. Ezra in the Bible also says Cyrus allowed the Jews to return. The Achaemenid dynasty was founded by Cyrus and it lasted for a long time. His son Cambyses later conquered Egypt, so the empire grew after Cyrus died. This shows that Cyrus had created a strong base for the empire. Cyrus’s conquest of Babylon also gave Persia control of a city that had long been a centre of administration and trade. This allowed his successors to build on the Babylonian system rather than replace it, which was part of why the empire could govern such different peoples. Cyrus contributed a lot to the empire. But Darius was responsible for many of the things that made the empire work, such as the administration and the roads. So Cyrus’s contribution was important, though not the whole picture.

After Cyrus died, his son Cambyses continued the empire. Cyrus was an important king who helped the Persians build a large empire. Cyrus also made the Persian kingdom larger than it had been, which was a lasting achievement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Darius I deserves the title to a considerable extent, though the title is partly a later construction. His reign from 522 to 486 BCE restored a fragmented empire, reorganised its administration and expanded its wealth, but his military failures in Scythia and Greece show the limits of his achievement. Persian royal inscriptions call him ‘great king’, a standard royal title. ‘The Great’ is a later designation, so the judgement must rest on what he achieved rather than on the label. Darius came to power after a succession crisis in which several rivals claimed the throne and revolts broke out across the empire. The Behistun inscription, carved on a cliff in western Iran, opens with the formula ‘I am Darius, the great king’ and records the revolts he suppressed, claiming nineteen battles in a single year. Whatever the exaggeration in that account, Darius restored the empire’s unity and presented himself as the legitimate heir of Cyrus and Cambyses. Few rulers faced such a crisis and recovered as completely. Darius’s administrative achievements are the strongest basis for the title. He divided the empire into satrapies, regularised tribute and taxation and introduced a gold coinage, the daric, which helped the empire trade and pay its armies. Persepolis, where the Fortification Tablets record rations, labour and goods in detail, shows a bureaucracy that could manage a large workforce. Herodotus, who was hostile to Persian rule, nonetheless describes the tribute arrangements in some detail and calls Darius a trader, a remark that reflects a Greek view of a king who measured the empire by its income. The title is harder to justify when his military record is considered. His expedition across the Danube against the Scythians in about 513 BCE failed to bring the nomadic forces to battle and cost his army heavily, according to Herodotus. The Ionian Revolt from 499 BCE required years of effort to suppress, and the Athenian victory at Marathon in 490 BCE was a serious defeat for the Persian army. Darius also planned a further expedition against Greece, which his son Xerxes carried out. Setbacks of this kind undermine the claim that he was a great conqueror, even if they did not destroy the empire. The title can also be measured against his successors. Xerxes carried out the invasion of Greece that Darius had planned, and the Greek sources often judge the Persian kings by their relations with Greece. Darius’s reputation in those sources owes much to Marathon, and the title would look different if the Persian evidence were given the same weight. This shows that the question of ‘greatness’ depends on the perspective of those who judge. Darius deserves the title to the extent that it recognises his restoration of the empire, the reorganisation of its government and the economic foundations he laid. His reputation as a conqueror is weaker because his campaigns in Scythia and Greece failed. The name ‘the Great’ is a later and largely European judgement, and it is best understood as a recognition of stability and administration rather than of military greatness. Judged on those terms, Darius deserves the title substantially, though not for the conquests that the name might suggest.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it separates ‘great king’ from ‘the Great’, weighs administration against the military failures, and reaches a qualified judgement. To go further, it could assess the Behistun claim of nineteen battles more critically against the Persian royal context.

sampleAnswers.answer: Darius I deserves the title to some extent because he was a very important king. He came to the throne after a crisis and restored the empire. He also created a good system of government, with satrapies and a standard tribute. The Behistun inscription shows that Darius defeated many rebels. It says he fought many battles in one year. He presented himself as a great king and the rightful heir of Cyrus. This suggests that he was successful in stopping the revolts. Darius also built Persepolis and introduced coins. These things show that the empire became more organised and wealthy under him, which is part of why people call him great. His use of royal inscriptions also shows an effort to present the monarchy as stable and legitimate. The Behistun inscription was carved beside a road where travellers would see it, which suggests that Darius wanted his authority to be publicly acknowledged across the empire, itself an achievement in a diverse state. However, Darius was not successful in everything. He failed to defeat the Scythians and he lost the battle of Marathon against the Greeks. These defeats mean he may not deserve the title completely.

sampleAnswers.answer: Darius I was a Persian king who came to power in 522 BCE. He built Persepolis and created a system of satrapies to govern the empire. markerNotes: The strongest answers define ‘significance’ before judging it, for example by the dynasty’s own survival or by its legacy, and then reach a judgement on each measure.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legal reforms were more significant than cultural reforms for the Qin dynasty during its short life, because the legal system made the state possible and the rulers’ control depended on it. Cultural reforms had longer-lasting effects, especially the standardisation of script, which outlasted the dynasty. The question therefore depends on whether significance is measured by the Qin’s own survival or by its legacy. On the first measure legal reforms were clearly more important, while on the second cultural reforms were more enduring. The legal reforms built on the reforms of Shang Yang in the state of Qin in the fourth century BCE. Qin law, enforced through a hierarchy of officials, collective responsibility among households and harsh penalties, made it possible to assess taxes, raise labour and conscript soldiers across a unified territory. The large public works of the dynasty, including the Great Wall and the palace and tomb complexes, depended on these powers. Legal texts found in tombs, such as the bamboo slips from Shuihudi, show how detailed the administration was, and the law gave the emperor a system for controlling officials. The cultural reforms were broader in intent. The first emperor standardised the writing system, adopting a small seal script for official use, and introduced common standards for weights and measures, the width of carriage axles and the coinage. These measures made administration and trade across the empire easier. The reforms also had a darker side: the burning of books and the burial of scholars in 213 and 212 BCE, recorded in the Shiji, aimed at removing rival traditions and centralising ideas. Such cultural policies showed that the state intended to shape not only conduct but also thought. The durability of these reforms is difficult to separate from the fall of the dynasty. The legal system’s severity contributed to unrest, and the rebellion of Chen Sheng in 209 BCE grew from conscription and forced labour that the legal system imposed. The Qin collapsed in 206 BCE, and its legal structure was partly moderated under the early Han, which kept an administrative framework and a degree of legalism but reduced the harshest penalties. The standardised script, by contrast, survived the collapse and remained a basis of Chinese unity, so the cultural reforms outlasted the dynasty that created them. The two kinds of reform also differed in their reach. The legal system applied to officials and households across the state, and its enforcement shaped daily life through taxes, labour and punishment. The cultural measures reached a smaller and more literate audience at first, but over time the script and standard weights and measures affected commerce and administration across the empire. This difference in reach is part of why the legal reforms shaped the dynasty’s fate while the cultural reforms shaped its legacy. Legal reforms were more significant for the Qin dynasty itself, because they gave the state the power to unify, to fight wars and to build, and their harshness is part of the reason the dynasty fell quickly. Cultural reforms had a greater and longer legacy, because the standard script and standard measures outlived the Qin. The Qin’s significance for the later Chinese state therefore rests largely on its cultural unification, while its significance as a political system depended on the legal foundations. To the extent that the question asks about the dynasty’s own period, legal reforms were the more significant.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it defines significance on two measures, weighs specific legal and cultural reforms against each other, and links both to the dynasty’s fall and legacy. To go further, it could assess the burning of books as a cultural measure with a more precise account of its intended targets.

sampleAnswers.answer: The legal reforms and the cultural reforms were both important to the Qin dynasty. The legal reforms came from Shang Yang’s earlier changes in the state of Qin, and they gave the government control over taxes, labour and soldiers. Without them the Qin could not have built the walls and palaces that the dynasty needed. The cultural reforms standardised things across the empire. The script was made uniform, and weights, measures and coins were also standardised. These changes made administration easier and helped trade. The burning of books in 213 BCE shows the government also wanted to control ideas. The Qin did not last long. The legal system was harsh, people rebelled against conscription and forced labour, and the dynasty fell in 206 BCE. The Han dynasty kept some of the Qin system but changed the harsh punishments. The legal reforms also had a clear purpose in the state’s competition with rival kingdoms. Strict law and collective responsibility made it easier to mobilise resources in war, and Qin used these powers to defeat its rivals in the Warring States period. The cultural reforms were less about winning wars than about holding the empire together afterwards. The standardised script lasted longer than the Qin dynasty. This suggests that the cultural reforms were more important in the long run. However, the legal reforms were important for the Qin itself, because they made the state work while it lasted.

The Qin reforms were also remembered later as a model of strong government, which shows their continuing influence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The empress dowagers made real contributions to the Han dynasty, though their influence varied greatly and was often judged harshly by male historians. Their most important contribution was to maintain continuity at court during periods when emperors were young or weak, but some used their position to advance their own families. The contributions were therefore mixed, and the judgement depends on whether stability or the interests of a family are given priority. The most powerful was Empress Lü, widow of the founder Gaozu. After her son Emperor Hui died in 188 BCE, she ruled as regent for the young emperors who followed until her death in 180 BCE. She appointed members of her own family to high posts and attempted to secure the Lü clan’s position, a policy that the Shiji, in its annals of Empress Lü, portrays as dangerous for the Liu house. Her regency preserved the court’s stability and kept the structures of the new dynasty in place, but after her death the Lü were overthrown by officials and Liu relatives, which suggests that her policy had made enemies. Empress Dou, consort of Emperor Wen and mother of Emperor Jing, was influential during the reigns of her husband and son, and into the reign of Emperor Wu. Her preference for Huang-Lao thought, which favoured quietist government, is recorded in later sources, and she is said to have opposed Confucian-minded officials who wanted to reform the court. Her influence blocked some of the reforms that Wu’s advisers proposed in the 130s BCE, but her death in 135 BCE removed the obstacle and allowed the emperor to pursue more active policies, including the promotion of Confucian scholars. Her contribution was a conservative one: she protected existing policies while delaying change. The contributions of the empress dowagers can be evaluated in two ways. Stability was the most important: Empress Lü kept a dynasty with young rulers on its throne, and Empress Dou prevented sudden changes during a period when the empire was still consolidating. Against this, both women used their positions to shape appointments and policy, and the historians who recorded their careers, writing within a male and Confucian tradition, portrayed them as threats to legitimate rule. Their reputations therefore say as much about later perspectives on women’s power as about their actual decisions. The empress dowagers’ influence also shows the limits of imperial authority. The dynasty depended on a small circle of relatives and officials, and when an emperor was young or weak the court needed someone to hold it together. The women who filled this role were those closest to the throne, but their authority was provisional and could be challenged by officials and other members of the imperial family. Their careers therefore show how the Han system relied on personal networks as well as on formal institutions. Overall, the empress dowagers were significant to the Han, particularly in providing continuity during succession crises and in shaping the pace of reform. Lü Zhi’s regency sustained the dynasty in its early years, while Dou’s influence slowed the move towards more active government. Their contributions are most accurately evaluated as mixed rather than simply negative or positive, and the record of their achievements is shaped by the sources that judged them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it evaluates two empress dowagers on stability and political interest, uses the Shiji and later perspectives as evidence, and reaches a clearly argued judgement. To go further, it could assess the Confucian reforms of Emperor Wu more precisely against Dou’s influence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The empress dowagers had a significant role in the Han dynasty because they were often in charge when emperors were young. Empress Lü ruled as regent after the death of Emperor Hui in 188 BCE and held power until her death in 180 BCE. She gave important positions to members of her family, as the Shiji records. Empress Dou was also influential. She was the mother of Emperor Jing and had influence during the early reign of Emperor Wu. She supported Huang-Lao ideas and is said to have opposed the Confucian officials who wanted reforms. The empress dowagers helped keep the dynasty stable, since their presence prevented sudden changes in government. However, they could also block reforms and favour their own families. Historians who wrote about them were often critical. Empress Lü’s regency also shows a dynasty adjusting to succession problems. Who held authority during a minority was a recurring weakness of the early Han, and her regency offered a way to keep the throne in the family while the young rulers grew up. The Lü clan’s fall suggests, however, that personal networks could become a threat when they were used against the wider court. Overall, the empress dowagers made some contributions to the Han, but their influence was mixed. They mostly helped stability but were sometimes a problem for the emperors.

sampleAnswers.answer: Miltiades’ role was important for the Athenian victory at Marathon in 490 BCE, but it was one of several decisive factors. He shaped the decision to fight, chose the tactics and secured the support of the other generals, while the Athenian hoplites, the Plataean contingent and the Persian army’s own choices also determined the outcome. Assessing his importance therefore requires separating the planning of the battle from the conditions that made it succeed. Herodotus gives Miltiades the central role in the decision to engage the Persian army. There were ten generals, the strategoi, who shared command, and the polemarch Callimachus had the casting vote. Herodotus reports that Miltiades persuaded Callimachus to vote for battle, which was decisive when the generals were divided. Miltiades’ experience made him persuasive: he had fought in the northern Aegean and had earlier ruled in the Chersonese, so his knowledge of Persian forces was greater than most generals’. Without his argument the Athenians might have waited for reinforcements, in the hope of Spartan help that in fact arrived after the battle. Herodotus describes Miltiades’ tactical arrangement in some detail. He drew up the Athenian and Plataean hoplites in a line matched to the Persian front, weakened the centre so that the wings could hold, and ordered a rapid charge across the open plain to reduce the time under Persian archery. The Persians broke through the centre, but the wings then turned inwards and destroyed the force that had advanced. This plan exploited the Persian reliance on archers and light troops, and it was not merely brave. The tactics suggest that Miltiades’ role was crucial, although the account is shaped by Athenian tradition. Other factors were equally important. The Plataeans sent about a thousand hoplites, which gave the Athenians numerical strength and political backing in the battle. The Athenian hoplites were well trained and disciplined, and their close formation told in hand-to-hand fighting in a way that the Persian light troops could not match. The Persians’ choice of landing at Marathon exposed their army to attack on the plain, and the Spartans arrived too late to take part. Hippias’ presence as a guide shows how the Persians relied on local knowledge that proved insufficient. The victory was thus the product of many factors. The importance of Miltiades can also be judged by what followed. The victory gave Athens prestige and encouraged the Athenians to see themselves as defenders of Greece, which shaped their relations with Sparta and the other Greek states in the decades that followed. Miltiades himself gained little lasting benefit: Herodotus reports that he was later prosecuted after a failed expedition to Paros, which suggests that credit for a victory did not always translate into political security. His role was therefore significant for Athenian self-image, but less so for his own career. Miltiades’ importance was substantial because he drove the decision to fight and devised the tactics that exploited the Persian formation. However, the victory depended on the discipline of the hoplites, the support of the Plataeans, the Persian choice of ground and the late arrival of the Spartans, which deprived the Athenians of help but also left them to win on their own. Miltiades was therefore a decisive figure in the victory, but his role was one of planning and persuasion within a wider set of conditions that made success possible. Judged as a whole, his role was important, though not sufficient on its own.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it assesses Miltiades’ importance against the hoplites, the Plataeans and the Persian choices, uses Herodotus’ account of the tactics, and reaches a qualified judgement. To go further, it could assess the Athenian tradition behind the account more explicitly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Miltiades was important for the Athenian victory at Marathon in 490 BCE. He was one of the generals and he had experience fighting Persians, which made his advice valuable. Herodotus says he persuaded the other generals to fight. The battle plan was also his. He arranged the Athenians in a line that matched the Persians, and then the Athenians charged across the plain. This surprised the Persians, who were used to archers. The plan helped the Athenians win. However, other factors mattered too. The Plataeans helped the Athenians, and the Athenian hoplites were well trained. The Spartans arrived too late to take part, so the Athenians had to win without them, and the Plataeans’ support was more significant than the Spartans would have been. The victory also depended on how the Athenian generals worked together. The decision to fight required agreement among commanders who were not always in accord, and Miltiades’ ability to win that agreement was part of his contribution. Without it the army might have waited in the city, which would have changed the outcome of the campaign. So Miltiades was important, though the battle depended on other things as well. He was a major part of the victory but was not the only reason for it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The activities of the Peloponnesian League were largely a response to Athenian imperialism between the 470s and 440s BCE, but they were not solely a response. Sparta’s leadership reflected long-standing concerns about its own position, including the helot population and its rivalry with Argos, which also shaped its policy. Athenian power provided the main pressure, but Sparta’s actions were also driven by internal and regional factors, so the response was real but not the sole explanation. In the years after the Persian Wars the Peloponnesian League was dominated by Sparta, which was reluctant to pursue a war of liberation and preferred to keep its alliance intact. When Athens turned the Delian League into an empire, Sparta’s response was cautious. Thucydides argues that the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta made war inevitable, which suggests that the League’s posture was a response to Athenian expansion. Yet Sparta’s concerns also included the helots: in 462 BCE, during a helot revolt, Sparta asked Athens for help and then sent the Athenian force away, an insult that Thucydides records as turning Athens towards Argos. The League’s activities in the 450s and 440s show a pattern of response. Spartan-led forces defeated the Athenians at Tanagra in 457 BCE, and in 446 BCE, after revolts in Boeotia and Megara, the Spartans invaded Attica and pressed Athens to accept the Thirty Years’ Peace of 446 or 445 BCE. In 432 BCE Corinth’s complaints at Sparta about Athenian actions against Potidaea and the Megarian decree prompted a Spartan assembly that led to war. These episodes suggest that Sparta responded to Athenian power with military and diplomatic action. Other activities cannot be explained by Athenian imperialism alone. Corinth and Megara had their own commercial interests and rivalries with Athens, which drew Sparta into conflicts that were not only about imperial control. Corinth pressed Sparta to act partly to protect its trade and its colonies, not only to counter an empire, and the League’s members often pursued their own disputes through Sparta’s authority. The League’s response was thus shaped by the interests of its members as well as by Athenian power. The League’s responses also show the limits of Spartan power. Sparta was reluctant to act against Athens without the support of its allies, and its decisions depended on the politics of its assembly and its anxieties about the helots. Thucydides’ account suggests that Sparta often acted only when Athenian expansion threatened its allies directly. This reluctance means that the League’s responses were shaped as much by the limits of Spartan willingness as by the pressure of Athenian power. To a considerable extent, the League’s activities were a response to Athenian imperialism, especially in the 450s and 440s, when Athenian expansion and the treatment of its allies provoked Spartan and allied action. However, Sparta’s concerns about the helots, the rivalries among its allies and Corinth’s commercial interests also shaped the League’s conduct. The response to Athenian imperialism was the most visible driver, but not the only one. The League’s activities are therefore best understood as a response filtered through its own internal divisions and interests.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it weighs Athenian imperialism against Sparta’s helot concerns and its allies’ interests, uses specific episodes and Thucydides, and reaches a qualified judgement. To go further, it could test Thucydides’ explanation of the war against the Corinthian speeches more directly.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Peloponnesian League was led by Sparta and was a response to Athenian imperialism in some ways. Athens built the Delian League into an empire in the 470s and 460s BCE, and Sparta was worried about this growth. Sparta fought Athens at Tanagra in 457 BCE, and in 446 BCE the Spartans invaded Attica. The Thirty Years’ Peace followed in 446 or 445 BCE. These events show that Sparta responded to Athenian power with military action. However, Sparta also had its own concerns, such as the helots, and Corinth had its own trade interests. So the League’s actions were not just about Athens. Athens’ own actions also shaped how Sparta responded. The empire’s use of tribute and its interference in allied cities gave Sparta’s allies reasons to complain, and Corinth in particular used these grievances to press Sparta to act. Sparta responded to a pattern of Athenian behaviour as much as to the empire itself. Overall, the League’s activities were partly a response to Athens, but they were also shaped by other things.

sampleAnswers.answer: The King’s Peace of 387 or 386 BCE was significant for developments in Greece between 387 and 362 BCE because it set the terms of diplomacy, gave Persia a role in Greek affairs and encouraged a system in which Sparta’s enforcement of autonomy generated new rivalries. Its importance lies less in the peace itself than in the ways its principles were used and contested. The period from 387 to 362 was shaped by the tension between autonomy and hegemony that the Peace created. The King’s Peace was brokered by the Spartan envoy Antalcidas with the support of the Persian king Artaxerxes II. Its terms recognised Persian control of the Greek cities of Asia Minor and Cyprus and declared that the other Greek cities should be autonomous, which Sparta presented as a principle of freedom but which in practice allowed Sparta to intervene against cities it chose to suppress. The Peace marked a new Persian role in Greek politics, since Persia could now set terms for the Greek states, and this role was used to balance Sparta and Athens against each other. Sparta enforced the Peace selectively and used it to strengthen its own position. It broke up the union of Mantinea in 385 BCE and seized the Theban citadel, the Cadmea, in 382 BCE, which was justified as an enforcement of autonomy but was widely seen as an abuse. Such actions were significant because they showed that the Peace could be turned against those who had accepted it, and they created resentment that Thebes later exploited. The Spartan garrison was expelled from Thebes in 379 BCE by exiles, which marked the start of Theban independence. Athens also responded to Spartan power by founding the Second Athenian Confederacy in 378 or 377 BCE. Its charter declared respect for the autonomy of its members, which echoed the Peace’s language, and the Confederacy allowed Athens to rebuild a sea power. The alliance was significant because it gave the Peace’s principles a new meaning: an anti-Spartan league could claim to defend autonomy. Thebes, meanwhile, built a Boeotian league and defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Leuctra ended Spartan hegemony and was the most important consequence of the Peace’s disputed principles. The Peace also shaped the political thinking of the Greek states. The principle of autonomy allowed cities to claim the right to govern themselves, and it could be invoked against Sparta, Athens or Thebes depending on who held power. Such a principle was flexible, and its meaning shifted with each new alliance. The King’s Peace therefore created a language of diplomacy that outlasted the Peace itself, and its significance for 387 to 362 lies partly in the arguments it made possible. The King’s Peace was significant mainly as the framework within which these conflicts took place. It legitimised Persian involvement, justified Spartan interventions and gave later powers a principle to invoke. Its effects were determined by how Sparta, Athens and Thebes used the principle of autonomy, and the collapse of Spartan hegemony at Leuctra showed that it could not secure lasting order. Between 387 and 362 BCE the Peace was therefore highly significant for the shape of Greek politics, though its significance lay in the disputes it generated rather than in the stability it provided.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 21–25 row: it assesses the Peace by its effects, shows how autonomy was used and contested by Sparta, Athens and Thebes, and reaches a clear judgement. sampleAnswers.answer: The King’s Peace of 387 BCE was important for Greece between 387 and 362 BCE because it set the rules for relations between the Greek states. It was brokered by Persia and Sparta and said the Greek cities should be independent. Sparta used the Peace to control other states. For example, Sparta broke up Mantinea and seized the Cadmea in Thebes in 382 BCE. This made other states angry, and Thebes later rebelled. Athens formed a new alliance in 378 BCE. This was partly a response to Sparta’s power. The Thebans then defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE, which showed that the Peace did not keep Sparta in charge. The Peace also affected Athens, which had lost its empire after the Peloponnesian War and had to rebuild its position under the Peace’s terms. The later revival of Athenian sea power through a new confederacy shows how the Peace left Athens room to act once Spartan power was stretched. So the King’s Peace was significant because it led to these events, although other things also caused them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Philip II was a highly successful Macedonian king, and by the standards of his time his achievements were exceptional. He restored a kingdom that was close to collapse, built an army that could defeat the Greek city-states, and laid the foundations for his son’s conquest of Persia. His success was not complete, however. His control over Greece rested on force and alliances that depended on his personal authority, and his assassination left his kingdom to a succession crisis. Philip came to the throne in 359 BCE in a kingdom threatened by Illyrian and Thracian enemies and by rival claimants, and he acted quickly to secure his position. He first served as regent for his nephew and then took the throne himself, using the army’s support to deal with rivals. His kingship drew on Macedonian traditions of personal leadership, and his skill as a commander and diplomat allowed him to build a stable state from a fragile inheritance. Philip’s reforms of the army were central to his success. He developed the phalanx with longer spears, the sarissa, and professional soldiers who were paid and trained, which gave the Macedonian army a flexibility that combined infantry and cavalry. His expansion followed: Amphipolis was taken in 357 BCE, Methone in 354 BCE, where he lost an eye, and the Chalcidian city of Olynthus in 348 BCE. These conquests secured Macedonia’s resources, especially timber and silver, and made Philip the dominant power in the north Aegean. Philip’s relations with Greece were built on diplomacy as well as force. The Peace of Philocrates in 346 BCE recognised his position, and he used the Third Sacred War to extend his influence into central Greece. The decisive victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE over the Athenians and Thebans brought the main Greek resistance under his control, and the League of Corinth in 337 BCE gave him a formal leadership of Greece. Yet Philip’s position depended on his army and on the willingness of Greek states to accept his terms, and Demosthenes’ opposition shows that resistance remained strong until the end. Philip’s success also depended on his handling of his court and his neighbours. He used marriage alliances, rewards and the threat of force to bind the Macedonian nobility and the peoples of the north to his rule, and his diplomacy with Thessaly and Thrace gave him security while he campaigned in the south. These arrangements show that his kingship was more than military strength: it was a system of loyalty that held the kingdom together and allowed his conquests to be sustained. Philip’s limits were significant. His attempts on Perinthus and Byzantium in 340 BCE failed, and his Greek policy was never fully accepted. His assassination in 336 BCE, at the wedding of his daughter at Aegae, showed that his court was not secure, and the succession passed to Alexander without a settled structure. Still, Philip’s achievements were remarkable: he transformed a weak kingdom into the strongest power in the Greek world and created the army and resources that Alexander used. Judged as a king, his success was very substantial, though his greatest ambitions were completed by his son.

sampleAnswers.answer: Philip II was a successful Macedonian king because he made Macedon the strongest state in Greece. He came to the throne in 359 BCE when the kingdom was in trouble, and he dealt with rivals and enemies. His army reforms were important. He trained a phalanx with long spears and paid his soldiers. This army allowed him to win battles, such as the battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, where he defeated the Athenians and Thebans. Philip also took many cities, including Amphipolis and Olynthus, and he gained control of silver mines. He also made a treaty with Athens in 346 BCE. These achievements show he was a successful king. His reign was also significant for the way he used Macedon’s resources. Control of mines and the revenue from new territories gave him money to pay the army and to outlast his rivals. This financial basis is one reason his achievements lasted beyond the campaigns that won them. However, Philip was murdered in 336 BCE, so his plans were not completed. Alexander then carried them out. So Philip was successful, but his son achieved the most.

sampleAnswers.answer: The optimates and populares were significant as the main political labels of the late Republic, though they were less rigid than the labels suggest. The optimates defended the authority of the Senate and the traditional leadership of the aristocracy; the populares were leaders who sought popular support, often through the assemblies and the tribunes. Their significance lies in the way the labels shaped alliances and hostilities, rather than in fixed parties with programmes. The distinction explains much of the period’s conflict, but it must be used with care. The optimates were significant because they gave the Senate a coherent defence against individuals who used popular support to gain power. Cicero, who spoke for the boni, the good men of the Senate, opened his prosecution of Catiline with the words ‘How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?’, and his suppression of the conspiracy in 63 BCE was a defence of senatorial authority. Cato the Younger was the most uncompromising defender of the Senate, and his opposition to Pompey’s arrangements and to Caesar’s consulship of 59 BCE shows the optimates’ role in resisting personal power. Their significance was greatest when they could unite behind the Senate’s authority. The populares were significant because they challenged the Senate’s monopoly of political initiative. Caesar, as consul in 59 BCE, used a popular assembly to pass land laws, and he allied with Pompey and Crassus in the First Triumvirate. Clodius, as tribune in 58 BCE, passed laws that provided grain and exiled Cicero, and his gangs were a form of popular mobilisation. The populares were not a unified movement, and several of them, including Clodius and Caesar, were themselves members of the aristocracy who used popular methods for personal ends. Their significance was in demonstrating the power of the assemblies and the tribunate when the Senate was divided. The labels should not be overstated. Pompey moved between the two camps, allying with the populares in the 60s BCE and with the optimates after 52 BCE, and many senators supported popular measures for their own advantage. The optimates and populares were therefore coalitions and styles of politics rather than settled parties. The labels were significant, but they served political argument as much as they described fixed groups. The labels also matter for how the sources were written. Cicero’s speeches and letters use the language of the good men against popular leaders, and his portrayal of his opponents shapes how historians have read the period. Caesar’s own commentaries present him as a defender of the tribunes and the people, which gives a different account of the same conflicts. Historians must weigh both perspectives, and the significance of the labels depends partly on who is using them. The optimates and populares were significant because they framed the political conflicts that brought down the Republic. They gave the Senate a defence and gave ambitious leaders a means of challenging it, and the failure of the optimates to accommodate Caesar, together with the populares’ use of the assemblies and the tribunate, combined to drive the crisis of 49 BCE. Their significance was real, but it was as political language and loose alliances rather than as organised parties, and historians who treat them as parties risk exaggerating their coherence.

To go further, it could assess the role of the tribunate in the populares’ success more precisely.

sampleAnswers.answer: The optimates and populares were important political groups in the late Republic. The optimates supported the Senate and the populares supported the people and the assemblies. These groups affected how politicians behaved. Cicero was an optimate who defended the Senate. He opposed some popular laws and he suppressed the Catilinarian conspiracy in 63 BCE. Cato was also an optimate and he was strongly against Caesar. Caesar and Clodius were populares. Caesar passed land laws as consul in 59 BCE, and Clodius passed a law on grain as tribune in 58 BCE. These men used popular support to challenge the Senate. The labels also shaped how contemporaries acted. Politicians who wished to be seen as defenders of the Senate could oppose popular laws, while those who sought popular support could use the tribunes to pass measures the Senate disliked. The labels gave the arguments a shared vocabulary even when the men using them were pursuing their own ambitions. The labels were not always clear, because Pompey changed sides and some senators supported popular laws too. The two groups were important, but they were not fixed parties.
